transcript.content: Hello. I'm glad you're here today. What brings you in to see me?

Everyone keeps telling me I’m too thin and need to gain weight, but I honestly don’t see what the big problem is with my size right now. My doctor and my family are the ones who insisted I come, but I feel like they are overreacting.
How do you feel about the idea of gaining weight, and do you worry a lot about your body shape or size?

To be honest, the idea of gaining weight panics me; even thinking about eating bread or rice makes my chest get tight because I picture my face and stomach puffing up overnight. Instead, my current size feels like a quiet victory because I feel lean, wiry, and much sharper than others on the job site. I just don't see why everyone thinks my weight is such a dangerous problem.
To help me get a clearer picture of your physical health, could you share your current height and weight, and let me know if you've recently lost a significant amount of weight?

I don't know my exact height and weight off the top of my head, but I have definitely lost weight over the last few years. My work pants from ten years ago are hanging off me and my tool belt keeps sliding down, but I see that as a positive thing because it makes me feel lighter and sharper. I really don't see it as a cause for concern.
Have you noticed any changes in your hormone-related health, such as a significant drop in your sex drive or, if applicable, your menstrual periods stopping?
I went through menopause quite a few years ago, so my periods aren't really a factor anymore. As for my sex drive, I haven't really thought about it or noticed any changes lately.
Could you give me a rough estimate of your current weight and height, or tell me about how many pounds you have lost overall?

I don't actually know my exact weight or how many pounds I've lost because I don't weigh myself regularly. All I can really tell you is that my clothes and my tool belt are very loose on me now. I don't have any specific numbers to give you.
Did the doctor who insisted you come here mention what your current weight or Body Mass Index (BMI) is, or tell you that it is dangerously low?

Yes, my doctor did say my weight was dangerously low and was really worried about my lab results, which is why she insisted I come here. I don't recall her mentioning a specific BMI number—if she did, I didn't really pay attention because I felt she was overreacting. From what I see in the mirror, I just look lean, wiry, and strong, not dangerously thin.
What specific methods do you use to keep your weight down, such as avoiding certain foods, skipping meals, or exercising excessively?

Most days I just have coffee in the morning, maybe an apple or some nuts mid-day, and a small bowl of soup at night. I avoid heavy foods like rice or bread because they make me feel panicky, and if my daughter is watching, I'll just move the food around my plate to look like I've eaten. That is really the extent of it.
Have you noticed any other physical changes lately, such as feeling cold all the time, dizziness when you stand up, or your skin becoming very dry?

I haven't really noticed feeling particularly cold, dizzy, or having dry skin. However, I have been getting worn out and fatigued much more easily than I used to. It's gotten to the point where I have to take more breaks in the workshop lately.
Besides restricting your food, have you ever used other methods to control your weight, such as making yourself throw up, using laxatives or diet pills, or exercising excessively?
No, I've never done anything like making myself throw up, taking laxatives, or using diet pills. I do some regular cycling and tai chi to stay active, but it is nothing extreme.
You mentioned your work pants from ten years ago are hanging off you now. Do you happen to remember what your weight was back then when those pants fit you normally?
I really don't remember the exact number, as I didn't keep track of my weight back then. I just know that those pants used to fit me perfectly.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits all core clinical features of Anorexia Nervosa (F50.0). She has significant, self-induced weight loss driven by severe restriction of food intake (avoiding bread/rice, eating minimal portions) and active avoidance of 'fattening' foods. She demonstrates a profound dread of weight gain ('panics me') and body-image distortion, viewing herself as 'lean, wiry, and strong' despite her doctor stating her weight is 'dangerously low' with concerning lab results. Although amenorrhea cannot be assessed due to her postmenopausal status, ICD-10 specifies that for postmenopausal onset, endocrine changes are not clearly manifest, thereby keeping F50.0 as the primary diagnosis over F50.1.
